analysis.one_liner: Temporarily eliminates federal income tax on long-term capital gains for individuals.
analysis.headline: The bill to make capital gains tax-free for three years never got a hearing or vote, dying in the Ways and Means Committee with only two cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made all long-term capital gains — profits from selling stocks, real estate, and other assets held over a year — completely tax-free for individuals for tax years 2002 through 2004 [S2, S3]. Wages would still be fully taxed, but nothing held in investments would be for those three years. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: People who sell assets at a profit — stocks, businesses, real estate, and other investments held longer than a year — would pay zero federal tax on those gains for three years [S2, S3]. Since capital gains flow overwhelmingly to the wealthiest households, the tax-free window would deliver its largest savings to high earners with big investment portfolios; an investor who realized a $1 million gain would keep roughly $150,000–$200,000 more than under the rates then in effect. The bill applies only to noncorporate taxpayers, so it is a benefit for individuals with gains, not the 60% or so of households whose income is almost entirely wages and who have little or no capital gains income to shelter [S2, S3].

how_it_helps.text: Adds a new section to the tax code excluding from gross income any gain that would otherwise be long-term capital gain for noncorporate taxpayers, so individuals owe no federal income tax on profits from selling assets held over a year [S3].

Applies to taxable years beginning in 2002, 2003, or 2004, and repeals the existing Section 1202 small-business stock exclusion for those years because the new blanket exclusion covers everything it did [S2, S3].
Is retroactive to 2002, so taxpayers who already paid tax on 2002 gains could file for refunds [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would lose all revenue from long-term capital gains for three years, with the shortfall made up by other taxpayers, by borrowing, or by future cuts. The burden would land on everyone who does not own significant appreciated assets — most wage earners — since the tax on their pay would be unchanged while the tax on wealth's preferred income stream disappeared [S2, S3].

drawbacks.text: The revenue loss is large and one-sided: wages would be taxed in full while a three-year window made profits from selling stocks, businesses, and property entirely tax-free, and capital gains are concentrated among high-income households [S2, S3].

A temporary, time-limited exemption invites distortions rather than investment: holders can delay sales into the tax-free window, then shift sales elsewhere, and retroactivity to 2002 rewards transactions already completed rather than encouraging anything new [S3].

By superseding the Section 1202 exclusion for the covered years, it would repeal a targeted break for small-business stock investors and replace it with a blanket break that helps every large asset holder [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrowly distributed: an investor selling an appreciated asset in 2002–2004 would keep every dollar of the gain tax-free [S3]. The cost is a large, retroactive revenue giveaway tilted toward the households that already own most appreciated assets, at a time when the alternative — taxing investment income at lower but still meaningful rates — was already on the table in 2003. The temporary design makes it worse, not better: it changes when people sell rather than whether they invest, and it hands a windfall to sales already made. Weighed honestly, this is a tax cut for concentrated wealth paid for by everyone else's future taxes or debt.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Johnny Isakson introduced the Capital Reinvestment Act of 2003 on January 29, 2003 [S1, S5].
Two Republican colleagues signed on as cosponsors [S4].

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day and never received a hearing, a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote; the record shows no action after the referral [S5].
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers kept the status quo: no three-year capital gains tax holiday was enacted, so the Treasury did not forgo that revenue and wage earners were not left covering the difference. Investors who hoped to sell assets entirely tax-free in 2003–2004 lost that opportunity.

for.name: Johnny Isakson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for tax bills
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — and the bill never reached the House floor

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill, and it never progressed far enough for a floor vote to reveal a broader split.

industries.note: They would have been the direct beneficiaries of a three-year zero rate on long-term capital gains, and the bill's death means they kept paying tax on realized gains [S2, S3]. Their gain would have come at public cost: forgone federal revenue that other taxpayers or future borrowing must cover.
A tax-free window can spur asset sales and fund flows, so managers and brokers stood to earn fees on a wave of transactions timed to the exemption. Its failure means no such windfall [S2, S3].
